name: Blue Purple
lede: Blue Purple is a vivid, electric violet-blue, a plain description that the books use for a place on the color wheel and for a whole class of pigments.

sections.title: A place on the wheel
sections.body:
Blue purple is a description more than a name, and no one coined it. Paterson's twelve-hue wheel puts blue-purple between [[blue]] and [[purple]] [1]. Our swatch is the screen sense, a vivid violet 6.7 units from ISCC-NBS vivid violet, and it comes from the xkcd survey of 2010 [2]. The survey's own raw value is a bluer, more intense #5A06EF [2].

Nearby names are [[blurple]], [[burple]], [[bluey-purple]] and [[purplish-blue]] [2]. The Google Books curve for the phrase rises from about 1850 and peaks in 1930 [2].

sections.title: Blue-purple in the pigment books
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium sorts its entries into color classes, and Blue-Purple is one [3]. The class gathers [[flower:logwood|logwood]], the lichen dye [[flower:lichens-orchil|orchil]] and its coloring matter orcein, the mineral glaucophane, the indigoid dyes and several cobalt phosphates and arsenates [3]. They share a hue, not a chemistry.

The older sense differs. Until Newton, the usual order of colors ran white, yellow, red, green, blue, purple, black, and purple was thought a mixture of blue and black [4]. The Hebrew *tekhelet* is read as blue or blue-purple, though translations are imprecise and few textiles survive [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive has this color over 1 per cent of its canvas, as photographed [2]. That describes this archive, not painting as a whole. A saturated electric violet is mostly a screen color and a synthetic-dye color, and our nearest fashion match is the aniline craze of the 1850s and 1860s [2].
